plate_findings.evidence: Progressive nasal bone and palate resorption

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Panel A shows the patient P3 at age 9 presenting with initial facial skin lesions, consistent with the chronological progression of MHC class I deficiency. B: Panel B shows progressive skin lesions and early nasal bone destruction at age 12, consistent with clinical progression of MHC class I deficiency. C: Panel C illustrates severe tissue destruction, nasal bone and palate resorption, and lip loss at age 17, reflecting advanced clinical progression of MHC class I deficiency.

(B) Nasal bone destruction and progression of lesions at age 12. (C) Progressive nasal bone and palate resorption, upper lip tissue loss, worsening skin lesions, and prosthetic nose implantation at age 17. The appearance of the skin wounds during active infection.
in_text_mentions: ures S3-6 ). Lesions were well-demarcated squamo-papular plaques, particularly on face and limbs. P3 developed refractory ulcers and facial tissue loss despite antibiotics, corticosteroids, surgery, ( Figure 1 ). He also did not response to mesenchymal stem cell therapy, either ( Supplementary Figures S7 , S8 ). He died at the age of 21 due to sepsis, which was secondary to skin infections. All skin lesions were confirmed histologically via biopsy. No bacteria, mycobacteria or fungal agents were found in the biopsies. Histopathological examination revealed granulomatous inflammation and vascul

Nasal septum perforation occurred in three patients (P2, P3, and P8). While nasal skin lesions were present in P2 and P3, they were absent in P8. In P3, progressive tissue destruction led to autoamputation of the nasal bone, cartilage, soft tissue, and most of the lips, severely affecting feeding and facial integrity. ( Figure 1 ).

panels.rationale: The figure is a clinical photograph of a real patient showing large, indurated plaques with ulcerations and crusting on the lower extremities. This presentation of severe cutaneous involvement is consistent with Type I bare lymphocyte syndrome (MHC class I deficiency), as stated in the article title and prior triage.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A shows dermatoscopic features of lesions, including central white scarring and yellow globules, in the context of MHC class I deficiency (Bare Lymphocyte Syndrome). B: Panel B shows dermatoscopic features of skin lesions, specifically yellow globules and peripheral telangiectatic vessels, presented as part of the patient presentation for MHC class I deficiency.
